questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvector of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvalue
questions.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}10 & 4 \\ -26 & -10\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-2\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 4 \\ -26 & -10\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10+2\text{i} & 4 \\ -26 & -10+2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(10+2\text{i}){x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -26{x}_{1}+(-10+2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A+2\text{i}I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{2}(5+\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ -\frac{1}{2}(5+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 5+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{5+\text{i}}{-2}=-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\text{i}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Complex Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
questions.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ -15 & -5\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=1-3\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=1-3\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ -15 & -5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6+3\text{i} & 3 \\ -15 & -6+3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(6+3\text{i}){x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -15{x}_{1}+(-6+3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1-3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-2+\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-2+\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=5,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{\text{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2+\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

 

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=1-3\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=1+3\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2-\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}=\frac{(5)(5)}{(-2+\text{i})(-2-\text{i})}=5.
$$

questions.problem:
Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ be linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 \\ 20 & 8\end{aligned}].$
Given that ${\lambda }_{1}=-4\text{i}$ is an eigenvalue of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-4\text{i}$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 \\ 20 & 8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-8+4\text{i} & -4 \\ 20 & 8+4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-8+4\text{i}){x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 20{x}_{1}+(8+4\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-2+\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-2+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

On the other hand, since ${\lambda }_{1}=-4\text{i}$ is a complex eigenvalue of $A,$ the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the  complex conjugate of ${\lambda }_{1}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\lambda }_{2}=\overset{―}{{\lambda }_{1}}=4\text{i}.
$$

Moreover, the corresponding eigenvector to ${\lambda }_{2}$ is

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\frac{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}=\frac{(-2+\text{i})(-2-\text{i})}{(1)(1)}=5.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Complex Eigenvector of a Matrix Given a Complex Eigenvalue
questions.problem:
If $v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2-2\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =2-2\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2-2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 2-2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1+2\text{i} & 5 \\ -1 & 1+2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-1+2\text{i}){x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}+(1+2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(2-2\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=(1+2\text{i}){x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}(1+2\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{1+2\text{i}}{1}=1+2\text{i}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Two Linearly Independent Complex Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix
questions.problem:
Given that ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} \\ {b}_{1}\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} \\ {b}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ are linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}],$
what is the value of $\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the eigenvalues of $A.$ To do that, we must solve the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 8 \\ -2 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-\lambda )-(-2)(8) & =0 \\ 1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +17 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{(-2)^{2}-4(1)(17)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{2\pm \sqrt{-64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{2\pm 8\text{i}}{2} \\  & =1\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =1\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, let's consider the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1+4\text{i}.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{1}I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+4\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+4\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4\text{i} & 8 \\ -2 & -4\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-4\text{i}{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}-4\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(1+4\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\text{i}{x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{2}\text{i}{x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=2,$ we get the eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ \text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Then, to compute the second eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=1-4\text{i}$, we simply compute the complex conjugate of ${\overset{―}{v}}_{1},$ and get

$$
{v}_{2}={\overset{―}{v}}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{1}{a}_{2}}{{b}_{1}{b}_{2}} & =\frac{(2)(2)}{(\text{i})(-\text{i})}=4.\end{aligned}
$$
